query: Earlier automotive-catalyst research reported that Cu–Ni catalysts can oxidize CO and hydrocarbons at lower temperatures without platinum-group metals, while Pd–Cu and Pt–Cu catalysts can resist poisoning by H2O and NO and enable oxidation below 150 °C. Multi-principal-element catalysts in nearly equiatomic ratios have also been explored as a framework for combining high activity, thermal stability, and reduced platinum-group-metal use. These prior results demonstrate individual capabilities but do not establish the combined performance demanded by increasingly stringent regulations: clean exhaust during transient and low-temperature operation, resistance to relevant poisons, and durability over a vehicle lifetime despite the mileage-related degradation observed in real-driving-emission studies. Starting from a near-equiatomic, multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst, what single intervention could address this combined activity, poisoning-resistance, and lifetime-durability problem without sacrificing low platinum-group-metal use? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention, explaining how it would work, predicting the change relative to the unmodified catalyst, defining the exhaust and aging conditions over which it should apply, citing supporting prior evidence, and specifying an experiment whose result would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled post‐synthesis redox treatment that induces reversible exsolution of sub‐nanometric Pt clusters from the near‐equiatomic high-entropy alloy catalyst will enhance low-temperature oxidation activity, improve resistance to poisoning by H2O and NO, and extend long-term durability—all without increasing the platinum load.
generation.material_initial_state: A near‐equiatomic, multi‐principal‐element automotive alloy catalyst containing low levels of platinum (and other PGMs) homogenously mixed in a high-entropy matrix.
generation.intervention: Expose the as‐synthesized catalyst to a mild, cyclic redox treatment (i.e. a controlled sequence of a reducing atmosphere at moderate temperature followed by a mild oxidative step) to trigger partial surface segregation (exsolution) of sub‐nanometric Pt clusters at pre‐existing nanoporous/grain-boundary sites.
generation.conditions: Simulated automotive exhaust conditions including transient and low‐temperature operation (<150 °C), exposure to water vapor (approximately 10 vol% or lower) and NO, as well as high‐temperature hydrothermal aging (up to ~850 °C for several hours).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a dynamic, nanoporous surface layer enriched in fine Pt clusters at grain boundary/nanopore sites, stabilized by the high-entropy matrix that lowers the overall surface free energy.
generation.mechanism: The redox cycling drives a reversible migration of Pt atoms to the catalyst surface where they form ultra‐small, well-dispersed clusters. This dynamic process maintains an optimal active site dispersion, limits sintering, continuously ‘self‐regenerates’ the active sites against poisoning species and carbon deposition, and hence improves both activity and durability under real-world automotive operating conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated catalyst is expected to show a lower light‐off temperature (e.g., reduced T10/T50 for CO/hydrocarbon oxidation by roughly 10–20% relative to the untreated baseline), considerably less deactivation in the presence of H2O and NO, and enhanced performance retention over long-term aging tests (e.g., similar or lower degradation over >338 hours of operation).
generation.baseline: The unmodified, near‐equiatomic high-entropy alloy catalysts exhibit moderate low-temperature oxidation activity and suffer more rapid deactivation from poisoning and thermal aging.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is anticipated to work only if the high-entropy matrix is sufficiently mixed to allow reversible exsolution. The benefits might diminish if the redox conditions are too aggressive (leading to irreversible sintering) or if the operating temperatures and poisoning loads far exceed typical automotive exhaust conditions.
generation.uncertainty: While evidence from studies on high-entropy oxide sinter-resistance (PMC12224923) and entropy-driven self-regeneration (PMC8505510) supports the feasibility of using redox cycling to stabilize Pt, the exact kinetics of Pt exsolution/dissolution and the quantitative improvements in low-temperature activity and durability remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of catalysts from the identical near‐equiatomic alloy synthesis. Subject one group to the controlled redox thermal cycling treatment while keeping the other group as a control. Test both groups under automotive exhaust simulation conditions that include transient low-temperature operation, water vapor and NO exposure, and accelerated high-temperature hydrothermal aging.
measurements: Light‐off curves (T10, T50, T100) for CO and hydrocarbon oxidation
Activity measurements in the presence of H2O and NO to gauge poisoning resistance
Long‐term stability tests (e.g., activity retention over 338 hours or analogous cyclic aging tests)
Microscopic evaluation (e.g., HAADF-STEM) of Pt cluster dispersion before and after aging
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the redox-treated samples do not show statistically significant improvements in low-temperature activity, poisoning resistance, and long-term durability compared to the untreated control—or if they exhibit signs of enhanced Pt agglomeration/sintering—the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this work, porous HEO nanofibers were elegantly produced via electrospinning technology, remarkably promoting the sinter‐resistance and water‐tolerance of supported sub‐2.6 nm Pt nanoparticles. Due to the high‐entropy effect, the surface free energy of the whole catalytic system was substantially reduced, thereby diminishing the thermodynamic driving force for sintering. As a result, 2.6‐nm Pt remained stable in size at 4.2 nm after aging even at 950 °C and maintained a size of 2.9 nm after aging at 850 °C in a humid atmosphere. In situ, HAADF−STEM revealed that the HEO nanofibers kept their nanopore structures up to 1000 °C. Therefore, the sinter‐resistant and water‐tolerant Pt/HEO catalytic system maintained 100% CO conversion for more than 338 h and withstood 35‐cycles reaction without declining even in the presence of vapor. This work reveals new insights into the high entropy‐driven sinter‐resistance of Pt species, offering new perspectives for exploring advanced catalytic systems with boosted durability.

AbstractThe sintering of Supported Transition Metal Catalysts (STMCs) is a core issue during high temperature catalysis. Perovskite oxides as host matrix for STMCs are proven to be sintering-resistance, leading to a family of self-regenerative materials. However, none other design principles for self-regenerative catalysts were put forward since 2002, which cannot satisfy diverse catalytic processes. Herein, inspired by the principle of high entropy-stabilized structure, a concept whether entropy driving force could promote the self-regeneration process is proposed. To verify it, a high entropy cubic Zr0.5(NiFeCuMnCo)0.5Ox is constructed as a host model, and interestingly in situ reversible exsolution-dissolution of supported metallic species are observed in multi redox cycles. Notably, in situ exsolved transition metals from high entropy Zr0.5(NiFeCuMnCo)0.5Ox support, whose entropic contribution (TΔSconfig = T⋆12.7 J mol−1 K−1) is predominant in ∆G, affording ultrahigh thermal stability in long-term CO2 hydrogenation (400 °C, >500 h).
